newsitem.title: THAILAND: No more victims found in worst Thai hotel fire.
newsitem.headline: No more victims found in worst Thai hotel fire.

text.p: Rescue workers searching the debris of Thailand's worst hotel fire spent several hours clearing the remains of a caved-in roof from a section of the 400-room Royal Jomtien Resort Hotel, but failed to find any more bodies on Sunday

Police said the total number of bodies recovered from the charred beach hotel after thre days stood at 90 including those of 10 foreigners. Another Hungarian woman and two Thais were still unaccounted for.
Provincial officials said they had not decided whether to continue the search on Monday.
Friday's fire, the latest in a series in Thailand, triggered a public outcry over poor enforcement of safety measures for high-rise and public buildings.
Irate Thais voiced anger on phone-in radio programmes over reports that locked fire exits of the hotel contributed to the high death toll.
The fire at Pattaya, about 200 kms (125 miles) southeast of Bangkok, was the second major disaster in recent years in which blocked emergency exits trapped dozens of hapless victims.
About 200 teenage workers perished in May 1993 after a fire broke out inside a locked warehouse at a toy factory at Nakhon Pathom just north of Bangkok.
In both incidents, the hotel and factory owners ignored safety standards and blocked emergency exits to protect their property from theft.

"Whatever excuses given by the hotel management (for locking the exits) were unacceptable," a member of the National Safety Committee told reporters on Sunday, adding that the Royal Jomtien Resort hotel should not have been allowed to have indoor fire exits on upper floors in the middle of the building.

Some 136 tourists and hotel guests died in north east Korat province in August 1993 after the Royal Plaza Hotel collapsed like a pack of cards. Officials later blamed the collapse on the building's earlier unlicensed modification.

A director of the Royal Jomtien hotel conceded on Sunday that the ill-fated 16-storey building, built in the late 1980s, was not equipped with sprinkler and smoke detecting systems. He said the hotel's fire alarms failed to go off on Friday.

The Nation newspaper said: "The safety laws are lax and are often not just ignored but also exploited through business greed...the hotel fire at Pattaya is another tragic example that the bubble did not just burst in the economy but also in the rules of law and quality of life."

Public safety experts voiced surprise that dozens of high-rise hotels and condominiums at an international resort town like Pattaya were served only by fire engines that could reach only up to seven storeys, about half the height of the Royal Jomtien hotel.
Officials of the Tourist Authority of Thailand said it took nearly four hours for a bigger fire engine from Bangkok to reach the scene.
Interior Minister Snoh Thienthong on Saturday blamed the hotel management for storing cooking gas tanks inside indoor kitchens.
Police said a gas explosion near the hotel's ground floor cafeteria triggered the fire.

"The gas tanks are like a time bomb kept inside the building," Snoh said, adding that he would call an emergency meeting of government agencies next week to boost safety measures at big public buildings.
Minister Snoh said a new government survey would be made to ensure that Bangkok high-rises have helicopter landing pads on rooftops.
